notes.front: What is coaxial cable (coax)?
notes.back: A cable with a centre conductor inside a surrounding conducting shield, separated by insulation, usually with an outer jacket.
notes.explanation: Coax is the usual feed line between an amateur transmitter and its antenna: it carries high-frequency signals with low loss.
notes.example: The cable from a mobile radio to its roof antenna is almost always coax with a screw-on connector at each end.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B03

notes.front: In coax, what is the dielectric?
notes.back: The insulating material between the centre conductor and the shield, such as solid plastic, foam or air.
notes.explanation: A voltage across the two conductors heats this insulation the way it would a capacitor's dielectric, and that heating wastes power, so the dielectric a cable uses sets part of its loss.
notes.example: Foam-dielectric coax, which holds a lot of air, has about 15% less loss than similar solid-dielectric cable.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 11 (NAVEDTRA 14183), Microwave Principles, p. 1-3; Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”

notes.front: What is hardline?
notes.back: Large, stiff coaxial feed line whose centre conductor may be copper tubing, with a foam, air or gas dielectric.
notes.explanation: Hardline is used on high-power transmitters, such as broadcast and high-power amateur stations; air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss of any feed line.
notes.example: A high-power broadcast transmitter feeds its antenna through gas-filled hardline.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable” (Hard line); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B11

notes.front: What is an RF connector?
notes.back: A plug or socket that joins coax to radios, antennas or other coax; common types are PL-259, BNC and Type N.
notes.explanation: Different types suit different frequencies, and outdoor connectors of every type need weather protection.
notes.example: A PL-259 is the common connector at HF and VHF; a Type N is preferred above 400 MHz.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B01, T9B06, T9B07

notes.front: What is a directional wattmeter?
notes.back: A power meter in the feed line that measures forward and reflected power separately, from which SWR is found.
notes.explanation: Because it senses power in each direction, it can show both output power and how much is reflected by a mismatch.
notes.example: With 100 W going forward and very little coming back, the SWR is close to 1:1.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “SWR meter”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C08

notes.front: What is an antenna analyzer?
notes.back: An instrument that measures an antenna system's impedance, used to check whether an antenna is resonant on the desired frequency.
notes.explanation: It is a common tool for fine-tuning and troubleshooting antennas and feed lines.
notes.example: Sweeping a new dipole with an antenna analyzer shows the frequency where it is resonant and the SWR is lowest.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Antenna analyzer”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C02

notes.front: What is an antenna tuner (antenna coupler)?
notes.back: A device that matches the antenna system's impedance to the transceiver's output impedance.
notes.explanation: Matching lets the transmitter deliver full power instead of cutting back for high SWR.
notes.example: A tuner between the radio and the feed line lets the transceiver see a match, and deliver full power, on a band where the antenna’s SWR is high.

notes.front: What is a dummy load?
notes.back: A device that stands in for the antenna so a transmitter can be tested without sending signals over the air.
notes.explanation: A typical RF dummy load is a 50-ohm resistor built not to act like a coil (non-inductive), mounted on a metal heat sink that sheds the heat: it turns the power into heat instead of radiating it.
notes.example: You adjust a new transmitter into a dummy load, so tests cause no interference.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C01, T7C03; Wikipedia, “Dummy load”

notes.front: What is a dipole antenna?
notes.back: An antenna of two conductors, end to end, with the feed line connected at the gap between them; usually half a wavelength long in total.
notes.explanation: Its length sets its resonant frequency (next card), and the half-wave dipole is also the basic element of many multi-element antennas.
notes.example: A wire strung between two trees and fed in the centre with coax is a typical HF dipole.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), Glossary (“Dipole Antenna”) and para 3-11; US Army, TM 11-666, Antennas and Radio Propagation (1953), para 95

notes.front: What is an antenna's resonant frequency?
notes.back: The frequency at which the antenna naturally resonates, set largely by its length; using it near that frequency is best.
notes.explanation: Like a plucked guitar string, a given length rings at a particular frequency; shorter elements resonate higher.
notes.example: Trimming the ends off a dipole raises its resonant frequency.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Dipole antenna”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A05

notes.front: What is a whip antenna, such as a quarter-wave vertical?
notes.back: A single straight, flexible rod or wire; the most common is the quarter-wave whip, about ¼ wavelength long.
notes.explanation: Whips are the usual antennas for handhelds and vehicles; longer 5/8-wave whips give more gain.
notes.example: On 2 m, a quarter-wave whip is about 19 inches long.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Whip antenna”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A08, T9A09

notes.front: What is antenna gain?
notes.back: The increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared with a reference antenna.
notes.explanation: An antenna cannot add power; it concentrates it in some directions at the expense of others.
notes.example: A beam that gives a stronger signal toward a distant station than a reference dipole in the same direction has gain.

notes.front: What is a beam antenna?
notes.back: An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction.
notes.explanation: Concentrating the signal gives gain toward the station you want, at the expense of other directions.
notes.example: A rotatable beam on a mast can be turned toward each station in turn.

notes.front: What is a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: A beam antenna with one driven element fed by the feed line, plus unfed (parasitic) elements: a reflector behind and directors in front.
notes.explanation: The parasitic elements pick up and re-radiate energy so that the radiation adds up in the forward direction; the main advantages are increased gain and a one-way pattern.
notes.example: A 2 m Yagi with a reflector, a driven element and several directors points its signal at one distant station.
notes.source: US Army, TM 11-666, Antennas and Radio Propagation (1953), paras 95 and 106; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 4 (“Yagi Antennas”)

notes.front: What is antenna loading?
notes.back: Electrically lengthening an antenna by inserting inductors (loading coils) in its radiating elements.
notes.explanation: A loading coil makes an electrically short antenna resonant at its operating frequency.
notes.example: A short HF mobile whip uses a loading coil so it resonates on a band where a full-size antenna would be far too long.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A02; Wikipedia, “Loading coil”

notes.front: The most common impedance of coax used in amateur radio is {{c1::50 ohms}}.
notes.explanation: Coax and dummy loads are both 50 ohms, so a dummy load matches the line.

notes.front: Why is coax the most common amateur feed line?
notes.back: It is easy to use and requires few special installation considerations.
notes.explanation: It is not the lowest-loss, the highest-power or the cheapest line; its advantage is convenience.

notes.front: As the frequency of a signal in coax increases, the loss {{c1::increases}}.
notes.explanation: So a cable run that is acceptable on HF loses more at UHF.

notes.front: RG-213 coax has {{c1::less loss}} than RG-58 at a given frequency.
notes.explanation: For a given frequency, RG-213 is the lower-loss choice; air-insulated hardline is lower still.

notes.front: Which type of feed line has the lowest loss?
notes.back: Air-insulated hardline.
notes.explanation: Air is the lowest-loss dielectric: foam coax uses as much air as possible to cut losses.

notes.front: What is the advantage of foam-dielectric coax over solid-dielectric coax?
notes.back: It has less loss per foot.
notes.explanation: Foam contains a lot of air, which lowers loss; Wikipedia puts it at about 15% less attenuation.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C11; Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”

notes.front: What three things are sources of loss in coaxial feed line?
notes.back: Water intrusion into connectors, high SWR and multiple connectors in the line.
notes.explanation: Keep connectors dry and few, and keep SWR low.

notes.front: The connector type most suitable for frequencies above {{c1::400 MHz}} is Type N.
notes.explanation: Type N is the RF connector for UHF and microwave work; the PL-259 is common at HF and VHF.

notes.front: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at {{c1::HF and VHF}} frequencies.
notes.explanation: They are not watertight and not preferred for microwaves; they are the everyday connector on HF and VHF radios.

notes.front: Which connectors used outdoors should be carefully taped against the weather?
notes.back: All of them: PL-259, BNC and Type N.
notes.explanation: Water in a connector causes loss and cable failure, whatever the connector type.

notes.front: The main cause of coaxial cable failure is {{c1::moisture contamination}}.
notes.explanation: Water that gets into coax raises its loss and ruins it.

notes.front: Why should a coax jacket resist ultraviolet light?
notes.back: UV can damage the jacket and let water into the cable.
notes.explanation: UV damage opens the jacket, and water then does the real damage.

notes.front: Power lost in a feed line is converted into {{c1::heat}}.
notes.explanation: Lost power is not radiated; it warms the cable.

notes.front: An SWR reading of {{c1::1:1}} indicates a perfect impedance match between antenna and feed line.
notes.explanation: The higher the ratio above 1:1, the worse the match.

notes.front: What does an SWR reading of 4:1 indicate?
notes.back: An impedance mismatch.
notes.explanation: SWR is a ratio, not a gain or loss in dB; 4:1 is far from the ideal 1:1.

notes.front: Why do most solid-state transmitters reduce output power as SWR rises beyond a certain level?
notes.back: To protect the RF output amplifier transistors.
notes.explanation: Reflected power can damage the output transistors, so the radio cuts back automatically; low output can be a sign of high SWR.

notes.front: Erratic changes in SWR are often caused by a {{c1::loose connection}} in the antenna or feed line.
notes.explanation: An intermittent contact changes the load from moment to moment.

notes.front: A typical RF dummy load is a {{c1::50-ohm non-inductive resistor}} mounted on a heat sink.
notes.explanation: 50 ohms matches the transmitter; non-inductive keeps it a pure resistance at radio frequencies; the heat sink gets rid of the power.

notes.front: Shortening a dipole {{c1::raises}} its resonant frequency.
notes.explanation: Shorter elements resonate at higher frequencies; lengthening or loading lowers the frequency.

notes.front: In which direction does a half-wave dipole radiate its strongest signal?
notes.back: Broadside to the antenna: at right angles to the wire.
notes.explanation: Radiation falls to zero off the ends, so a horizontal dipole favours the two directions square to it.

image.alt: Top view of a horizontal half-wave dipole with its radiation pattern: a figure of eight whose two large lobes point broadside (at right angles to the wire), with almost nothing off the two ends.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A10, and Wikipedia, “Dipole antenna”

notes.front: Why is a 19-inch vertical antenna often used on 2 m?
notes.back: It is a resonant quarter-wave.
notes.explanation: A 2 m wavelength is about 2 m (300 ÷ 146 MHz ≈ 2.05 m); a quarter of that is about 0.5 m, roughly 19–20 inches.

notes.front: What is the advantage of a 5/8-wavelength whip over a 1/4-wave whip for VHF or UHF mobile use?
notes.back: It has more gain.
notes.explanation: The longer whip has better directivity, which shows up as gain.

notes.front: Compared with a full-size quarter-wave antenna, what is the disadvantage of a handheld's short flexible antenna?
notes.back: It has low efficiency.
notes.explanation: Shortening an antenna below its natural length costs efficiency, so less of the power becomes signal.

notes.front: Using a handheld VHF radio inside a vehicle with no outside antenna reduces signal strength because of the vehicle's {{c1::shielding effect}}.
notes.explanation: The metal body blocks much of the signal; an externally mounted antenna avoids this.

notes.front: Of a 5/8-wave vertical, an isotropic antenna, a J-pole and a Yagi, which offers the greatest gain?
notes.back: The Yagi.
notes.explanation: A Yagi is a beam antenna that concentrates the signal in one direction. An isotropic antenna is only a reference for measuring gain, and a 5/8-wave vertical radiates equally in all horizontal directions.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A06; 47 CFR 2.1 (“Gain of an Antenna”); Wikipedia, “Whip antenna”

notes.front: Which of the following might be the cause of low RF power output from a solid-state transceiver?
notes.back: High SWR
notes.choices:
A) Poor amplifier noise figure
B) Poor amplifier linearity
C) Low SWR
D) High SWR
notes.choicesExplained: A: noise figure affects receiving, not output power. B: poor linearity causes distortion, not low output. C: low SWR is the good condition.
notes.explanation: High SWR makes a solid-state transceiver reduce its output to protect itself.

notes.front: What is the primary purpose of a dummy load?
notes.back: To prevent transmitting signals over the air when making tests
notes.choices:
A) To prevent transmitting signals over the air when making tests
B) To prevent over-modulation of a transmitter
C) To improve the efficiency of an antenna
D) To improve the signal-to-noise ratio of a receiver
notes.choicesExplained: B: modulation level is set at the transmitter, not by the load. C: it does not improve an antenna; it replaces one. D: it has nothing to do with receiving.
notes.explanation: A dummy load lets you test a transmitter without sending signals over the air.

notes.front: Which of the following is used to determine if an antenna is resonant at the desired operating frequency?
notes.back: An antenna analyzer
notes.choices:
A) A VTVM
B) An antenna analyzer
C) A Q meter
D) A frequency counter
notes.choicesExplained: A: a VTVM measures voltage. C: a Q meter measures component quality, not antenna resonance. D: a frequency counter measures a signal's frequency.
notes.explanation: An antenna analyzer measures the antenna system’s impedance across frequency and shows where the antenna is resonant, which is where its SWR is lowest.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C02; Wikipedia, “Antenna analyzer”

notes.front: What does a typical RF dummy load consist of?
notes.back: A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor mounted on a heat sink
notes.choices:
A) A low-voltage power supply and an AC relay
B) A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor mounted on a heat sink
C) A low-voltage power supply and a DC relay
D) A 50-ohm inductive reactance mounted in a shielded enclosure
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: power supplies and relays are not a load for RF. D: an inductive reactance would not be a proper 50-ohm resistive load.
notes.explanation: 50 ohms matches the transmitter and coax; non-inductive keeps it a plain resistance at RF; the heat sink carries away the power it turns into heat.

notes.front: What reading on an SWR meter indicates a perfect impedance match between the antenna and the feed line?
notes.choices:
A) 50:50
B) Zero
C) 1:1
D) Full Scale
notes.choicesExplained: A: SWR is not written 50:50. B: SWR cannot be zero; the minimum is 1:1. D: full scale suggests a very high SWR.
notes.explanation: SWR is the ratio of the highest to the lowest voltage along the line. With a perfect match nothing is reflected, the voltage is the same all along, and the ratio is 1:1.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C04; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), Glossary (“Standing-Wave Ratio”)

notes.front: Why do most solid-state transmitters reduce output power as SWR increases beyond a certain level?
notes.back: To protect the RF output amplifier transistors
notes.choices:
A) To protect the RF output amplifier transistors
B) To comply with FCC rules on spectral purity
C) Because power supplies cannot supply enough current at high SWR
D) To lower the SWR on the transmission line
notes.choicesExplained: B: spectral-purity rules are not the reason. C: the power supply is not the limit. D: cutting power does not change the SWR.
notes.explanation: The radio cuts power at high SWR to protect its RF output transistors.

notes.front: What does an SWR reading of 4:1 indicate?
notes.back: Impedance mismatch
notes.choices:
A) Loss of -4 dB
B) Good impedance match
C) Gain of +4 dB
D) Impedance mismatch
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: SWR is a ratio, not a gain or loss in dB. B: 4:1 is a poor match, not a good one.
notes.explanation: The further SWR rises above the 1:1 of a perfect match, the worse the match; 4:1 is far from it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C06, T7C04, T9B12

notes.front: What happens to power lost in a feed line?
notes.back: It is converted into heat
notes.choices:
A) It increases the SWR
B) It is radiated as harmonics
C) It is converted into heat
D) It distorts the signal
notes.choicesExplained: A: loss does not increase SWR. B: lost power is not radiated at all. D: loss weakens the signal rather than distorting it.
notes.explanation: The conductors’ resistance is never zero, so the current in them dissipates some energy as heat; the dielectric absorbs some power too.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C07; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 3 (“Losses in Transmission Lines”)

notes.front: Which instrument can be used to determine SWR?
notes.back: Directional wattmeter
notes.choices:
A) Voltmeter
B) Ohmmeter
C) Iambic pentameter
D) Directional wattmeter
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: voltmeters and ohmmeters do not measure SWR. C: iambic pentameter is a rhythm in poetry, a joke option.
notes.explanation: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power, from which SWR is found.

notes.front: Which of the following causes failure of coaxial cables?
notes.back: Moisture contamination
notes.choices:
A) Moisture contamination
B) Solder flux contamination
C) Rapid fluctuation in transmitter output power
D) Operation at 100% duty cycle for an extended period
notes.choicesExplained: B: solder flux is not the common cause. C: changes in power do not damage coax. D: continuous transmitting within ratings is not the cause.
notes.explanation: Water that gets into coax adds loss and ruins the cable, which is why connectors are taped outdoors.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C09, T9B08, T9B01

notes.front: Why should the outer jacket of coaxial cable be resistant to ultraviolet light?
notes.back: Ultraviolet light can damage the jacket and allow water to enter the cable
notes.choices:
A) Ultraviolet light can increase the resistance of the conductors
B) Ultraviolet light can increase losses in the cable’s jacket
C) Ultraviolet and RF signals can mix, causing interference
D) Ultraviolet light can damage the jacket and allow water to enter the cable
notes.choicesExplained: A: UV does not change the conductors' resistance. B: the jacket carries no signal, so its losses are not the issue. C: light and RF do not mix in the cable.
notes.explanation: A cracked jacket lets water in, and moisture is what ruins coax.

notes.front: What is an advantage of foam-dielectric versus solid-dielectric coaxial cable?
notes.back: It has less loss per foot
notes.choices:
A) It is more resistant to moisture contamination
B) It has higher voltage breakdown
C) It has less loss per foot
D) It has a better impedance match to 50 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: A: foam is not more moisture resistant. B: it does not have higher voltage breakdown. D: the dielectric type changes the loss, not the match; foam cable is no better matched to 50 ohms.
notes.explanation: Foam holds as much air as possible, and air loses less than solid plastic, so foam coax has about 15% less loss.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7C11; Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”

notes.front: What is a beam antenna?
notes.back: An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction
notes.choices:
A) An antenna built from square aluminum beams
B) An omnidirectional antenna invented by Clarence Beam
C) An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction
D) An antenna that focuses the signal into two intense rays
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not named after square aluminium beams. B: it is not omnidirectional, and there is no inventor called Beam. D: it favours one direction, not two rays.
notes.explanation: Concentrating the signal in one direction gives gain toward the station you want.

notes.front: Which of the following describes a type of antenna loading?
notes.back: Electrically lengthening by inserting inductors in radiating elements
notes.choices:
A) Electrically lengthening by inserting inductors in radiating elements
B) Inserting a resistor in the radiating portion of the antenna to make it resonant
C) Installing a spring in the base of a mobile vertical antenna to make it more flexible
D) Strengthening the radiating elements of a beam antenna to better resist wind damage
notes.choicesExplained: B: a resistor wastes power; it does not make an antenna resonant. C: a spring adds flexibility, not loading. D: strengthening elements is mechanical, not loading.
notes.explanation: A coil makes a short antenna act electrically longer, and a longer antenna resonates at a lower frequency.

notes.front: What is a disadvantage of a handheld radio transceiver’s short flexible antenna compared to a full-sized quarter-wave antenna?
notes.back: It has low efficiency
notes.choices:
A) It has low efficiency
B) It transmits only circularly polarized signals
C) It is more susceptible to receiver desensitization
D) It only works on analog signals, not digital ones
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is not circularly polarized. C: the drawback of the short antenna is its low efficiency, not greater receiver desensitization. D: antennas work for analog and digital signals alike.
notes.explanation: A short flexible antenna is far shorter than a quarter wave and is often made to resonate with a loading coil instead of full length; the price is low efficiency.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A04, T9A02; Wikipedia, “Whip antenna”

notes.front: Which of the following increases the resonant frequency of a dipole antenna?
notes.back: Shortening it
notes.choices:
A) Lengthening it
B) Inserting coils in series with radiating wires
C) Shortening it
D) Adding capacitive loading to the ends of the radiating wires
notes.choicesExplained: A: lengthening lowers it. B and D: coils and capacitive loading make it electrically longer, lowering the frequency.
notes.explanation: A practical half-wave antenna is about 142.5 ÷ MHz metres long, so the shorter the dipole, the higher the frequency it resonates on.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A05; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 3-8 (“Antenna Length”)

notes.front: Which of the following types of antennas offers the greatest gain?
notes.back: Yagi
notes.choices:
A) 5/8 wave vertical
B) Isotropic
C) J pole
D) Yagi
notes.choicesExplained: A: a 5/8-wave vertical radiates equally in all horizontal directions, so it does not concentrate power as a beam does. B: an isotropic antenna is a theoretical reference, not a high-gain antenna. C: the J-pole is not the beam antenna here; the Yagi is.
notes.explanation: The Yagi, a beam antenna, concentrates the signal in one direction, which gives it the greatest gain of those listed.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A06, T9A01; Wikipedia, “Whip antenna”

notes.front: What is a potential drawback of using a handheld VHF transceiver inside a vehicle that lacks an externally mounted antenna?
notes.back: Signal strength is reduced due to the shielding effect of the vehicle
notes.choices:
A) Signal strength is reduced due to the shielding effect of the vehicle
B) The bandwidth of the antenna will decrease, increasing SWR
C) The SWR might decrease, decreasing the signal strength
D) The handheld will overheat due to reflected power in the vehicle
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the problem is shielding, not antenna bandwidth or SWR. D: the handheld does not overheat from reflected power.
notes.explanation: The vehicle's metal body shields the handheld, reducing signal strength.

notes.front: Why is a 19-inch-long vertical antenna often used on 2 meters?
notes.back: It is a resonant quarter-wave
notes.choices:
A) It has high gain
B) It is a resonant half-wave
C) It is a resonant quarter-wave
D) It has low RF radiation exposure
notes.choicesExplained: A: a quarter-wave vertical has no special high gain. B: a half-wave on 2 m would be about 39 inches. D: its length is not chosen for RF exposure.
notes.explanation: A practical half-wave antenna is about 142.5 ÷ MHz metres long, about 0.98 m at 146 MHz; half of that, a quarter wave, is about 0.49 m, or 19 inches.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A08; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 3-8 (“Antenna Length”)

notes.front: What is an advantage of a 5/8-wavelength whip antenna for VHF or UHF mobile service compared to a 1/4-wave antenna?
notes.back: It has more gain
notes.choices:
A) It has more gain
B) It radiates at a higher angle
C) It has lower SWR
D) It has lower impedance
notes.choicesExplained: B: a 5/8-wave whip puts most of its signal into a low, horizontal lobe; its high-angle radiation is poor, not higher. C and D: lower SWR and impedance are not its advantage.
notes.explanation: The longer 5/8-wave whip concentrates more of its signal toward the horizon, which gives it more gain than a 1/4-wave whip.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A09; Wikipedia, “Whip antenna”

notes.front: In which direction does a half-wave dipole antenna radiate the strongest signal?
notes.back: Broadside to the antenna
notes.choices:
A) Equally in all directions
B) Off the ends of the antenna
C) In the direction of the feed line
D) Broadside to the antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A: a dipole is directional, not equal in all directions. B: radiation falls to zero off the ends. C: the feed line direction has nothing to do with the pattern.
notes.explanation: Radiation from a half-wave dipole is strongest at right angles to the wire and falls to almost nothing off its ends.

image.alt: Top view of a horizontal half-wave dipole with its radiation pattern: a figure of eight whose two large lobes point broadside (at right angles to the wire), with almost nothing off the two ends.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A10, and Wikipedia, “Dipole antenna”

notes.front: What is antenna gain?
notes.back: The increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared to a reference antenna
notes.choices:
A) The additional power that is added to the transmitter power
B) The additional power that is required in the antenna when transmitting on a higher frequency
C) The increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared to a reference antenna
D) The increase in impedance on receive or transmit compared to a reference antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A: an antenna adds no power to the transmitter's. B: gain is not extra power needed at higher frequencies. D: gain is not an impedance change.
notes.explanation: An antenna cannot add power; gain compares the power a reference antenna would need to give the same field strength in that direction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A11; 47 CFR 2.1 (“Gain of an Antenna”)

notes.front: Which of the following connectors should be carefully taped for weather protection when used outdoors?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) PL259
B) BNC
C) Type N
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one of the connectors; all are correct.
notes.explanation: PL-259, BNC and Type N connectors all need careful taping outdoors: water in a connector adds loss and ruins the cable, and the PL-259 in particular is not watertight.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B01, T9B08, T7C09, T9B07

notes.front: What is the most common impedance of coaxial cables used in amateur radio?
notes.back: 50 ohms
notes.choices:
A) 8 ohms
B) 50 ohms
C) 600 ohms
D) 12 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: 8 and 12 ohms are far below the 50 to 600 ohms of feed lines in actual use. C: 600 ohms is at the top of that range, not the common coax value.
notes.explanation: Radios, coax and dummy loads are all built around 50 ohms, so they match one another.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B02, T7C03; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 3 (“Characteristic Impedance”)

notes.front: Why is coaxial cable the most common feed line for amateur radio antenna systems?
notes.back: It is easy to use and requires few special installation considerations
notes.choices:
A) It is easy to use and requires few special installation considerations
B) It has less loss than any other type of feed line
C) It can handle more power than any other type of feed line
D) It is less expensive than any other type of feed line
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not have the lowest loss; hardline does. C: it is not the highest-power line. D: it is not the cheapest.
notes.explanation: Coax is easy to use and needs few special installation measures.

notes.front: What is the major function of an antenna tuner (antenna coupler)?
notes.back: It matches the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance
notes.choices:
A) It matches the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance
B) It helps a receiver automatically tune in weak stations
C) It allows an antenna to be used on both transmit and receive
D) It automatically selects the proper antenna for the frequency band being used
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not tune the receiver to stations. C: a transceiver already uses one antenna for both. D: it does not switch antennas.
notes.explanation: With a match, the transmitter can deliver full power instead of cutting back to protect its output transistors from high SWR.

notes.front: What happens as the frequency of a signal in coaxial cable is increased?
notes.back: The loss increases
notes.choices:
A) The characteristic impedance decreases
B) The loss decreases
C) The characteristic impedance increases
D) The loss increases
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: a coax cable’s characteristic impedance does not depend on frequency over its working range; its loss does. B: loss rises, not falls.
notes.explanation: Coax loss rises with frequency, so a cable run that is fine on HF loses more at UHF.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B05; Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”

notes.front: Which of the following connector types is most suitable as an RF connector for frequencies above 400 MHz?
notes.back: Type N
notes.choices:
A) PL-259
B) Type N
C) RS-213
D) DB-25
notes.choicesExplained: A: PL-259 is an HF and VHF connector. C: “RS-213” is not a connector (RG-213 is a cable). D: DB-25 is a computer data connector.
notes.explanation: Type N is the connector for the higher frequencies; the PL-259 is an HF and VHF connector.

notes.front: Which of the following is true of PL-259 type coax connectors?
notes.back: They are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies
notes.choices:
A) They are preferred for microwave operation
B) They are watertight
C) They are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies
D) They are a bayonet-type connector
notes.choicesExplained: A: they are not preferred for microwaves; Type N is. B: they are not watertight. D: they are not a bayonet-type connector.
notes.explanation: The PL-259 is the everyday connector on HF and VHF radios; for microwaves Type N is preferred.

notes.front: Which of the following is a source of loss in coaxial feed line?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Water intrusion into coaxial connectors
B) High SWR
C) Multiple connectors in the line
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one source of loss; all are correct.
notes.explanation: Each adds loss: water in the connectors, power reflected by a mismatch, and every extra connector in the line. Keep connectors dry and few, and keep SWR low.

notes.front: What can cause erratic changes in SWR?
notes.back: Loose connection in the antenna or feed line
notes.choices:
A) Local thunderstorm
B) Loose connection in the antenna or feed line
C) Over-modulation
D) Overload from a strong local station
notes.choicesExplained: A: thunderstorms cause static, not SWR changes. C: over-modulation distorts the signal but does not change the match. D: overload from a strong station affects the receiver.
notes.explanation: A loose contact changes the load from moment to moment, so the match, and with it the SWR, jumps about.

notes.front: What is the electrical difference between RG-58 and RG-213 coaxial cable?
notes.back: RG-213 cable has less loss at a given frequency
notes.choices:
A) There is no significant difference between the two types
B) RG-58 cable has two shields
C) RG-213 cable has less loss at a given frequency
D) RG-58 cable can handle higher power levels
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is a significant difference: loss. B: RG-58 does not have two shields. D: the keyed difference is loss at a given frequency, not higher power handling by RG-58.
notes.explanation: RG-213 has less loss than RG-58 at a given frequency.

notes.front: Which of the following types of feed line has the lowest loss?
notes.back: Air-insulated hardline
notes.choices:
A) 50-ohm flexible coax
B) Multi-conductor unbalanced cable
C) Air-insulated hardline
D) 75-ohm flexible coax
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: flexible coax, 50 or 75 ohm, loses more. B: multi-conductor unbalanced cable is not a low-loss feed line.
notes.explanation: Air is the lowest-loss practical dielectric: of the usual insulations, air loses least, then foam plastic, then solid plastic.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B11; Wikipedia, “Coaxial cable”

notes.front: What is standing wave ratio (SWR)?
notes.back: A measure of how well a load is matched to a transmission line
notes.choices:
A) A measure of how well a load is matched to a transmission line
B) The ratio of amplifier power output to input
C) The transmitter efficiency ratio
D) An indication of the quality of your station’s ground connection
notes.choicesExplained: B: output-to-input ratio is amplifier gain. C: it is not transmitter efficiency. D: it does not measure the station ground.
notes.explanation: A feed line is a transmission line: SWR shows how well its load, the antenna, matches it, and a mismatch reflects power back along the line.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B12; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), Glossary (“Standing-Wave Ratio”)

notes.front: PL-259 or Type N: which is the usual choice at HF and VHF, and which above 400 MHz?
notes.back: PL-259 at HF and VHF; Type N above 400 MHz.
notes.explanation: Outdoors, both should be carefully taped against the weather; PL-259s are not watertight.
notes.contrast: PL-259: HF/VHF. Type N: above 400 MHz.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9B06, T9B07, T9B01

notes.front: RG-58 or RG-213: which loses less at a given frequency?
notes.explanation: RG-58 has more loss than RG-213; for the lowest loss of all, use air-insulated hardline.
notes.contrast: RG-58: more loss. RG-213: less loss.

notes.front: Antenna tuner or antenna analyzer: which measures, and which matches?
notes.back: The analyzer measures an antenna's impedance and resonance; the tuner matches the antenna system to the transceiver.
notes.explanation: Use the analyzer to find out what the antenna is doing, and the tuner to make the transceiver see a match.

notes.front: Transmitting into a dummy load or into an antenna: which sends a signal over the air?
notes.back: Only the antenna; the dummy load turns the power into heat.
notes.explanation: That is why tests and adjustments are made into a dummy load: nothing is radiated, so no one is disturbed.
notes.contrast: Dummy load: heat, no signal. Antenna: radiates.

notes.front: A half-wave dipole and a beam antenna: how do their radiation patterns differ?
notes.back: A dipole radiates in two directions, broadside to the wire; a beam concentrates its signal in one direction.
notes.explanation: Concentrating the signal gives a beam, such as a Yagi, more gain in its chosen direction.
notes.contrast: Dipole: two broadside lobes. Beam: one main direction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T9A10, T9A01, T9A06
